newsitem.title: DUBAI: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - eyes on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Mideast Gulf oil outlook - eyes on Iraq.

text.p: Gulf oil traders will next week be watching how much oil Iraq will be exporting since its resumption of liftings to gauge the effect it will have on crude and product markets.
The first tanker under the second term of Iraq's oil-for-food deal began lifting crude at Ceyhan at 2100 GMT on Wednesday, a Turkish pipeline official said.
Iraq resumed pumping oil through the Iraq-Turkish pipeline to the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan early on Thursday, an Iraqi oil ministry source said.
Traders say the resumption of exports by Iraq, with the world's second largest crude reserves, could dampen world oil prices, which could filter through to product prices.
Traders are still waiting for signs of oil tankers making their way to Iraq's Mina al-Bakr export terminal.
They are due to start loading from al-Bakr in the northern Gulf on August 18, marking Baghdad's first crude exports from the Gulf since the last U.N. sales period expired in June.
Shipping sources said on Thursday there were no signs yet of tankers sailing through the Strait of Hormuz on route to al-Bakr, 12 miles (19 km) off Iraq's southern Fao peninsula.
The middle distillate market in the Gulf was mainly quiet in the week, with some regional refinery maintenance expected.
"The Gulf is a bit quiet at the moment. There are a few cargoes here and there, so jet is flattish to trading at a discount," said one Gulf trader.
Gas oil was also seen at a narrow premium or even discount to price quotes.
One trader said the Nepal Oil Corp tender to buy 0.5 percent gas oil for September was expected to be awarded at a discount.
Industry sources said the best offer for the tender was from German trader Mabanaft at around $176.99 a tonne.
Outright prices were mainly steady in the week with gas oil assessed at $20.65 a barrel fob on Thursday and jet at $21.25.
Traders said the absence of much business made predicting premiums difficult. "In the last few days there have not been very many deals done, so there is not much indication for premiums," one said.
They expected the market to remain oversupplied into September. "September is also a bit long," one said.
A 30-day maintenance shutdown at Saudi Aramco's Ras Tanura refinery was expected to start in the second half of August but traders said the impact on product supplies would be limited.
